blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.body: My name is Isamu, and during the summer of 2026, I had the opportunity to spend ten weeks interning at the California State Water Board through the Environmental Policy Internship (EPIC), a sponsored program that places undergraduate students in public-service positions to gain hands-on experience in environmental policy. The program is a partnership between the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability, the Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment, the Haas Center for Public Service, and Stanford in Government. During my time at the State Water Board, I had the opportunity to speak with E. Joaquin Esquivel, Chair of the California State Water Board, whose perspective on the interconnectedness of California’s water and energy systems inspired me to explore the Water-Energy Nexus. Building on that conversation, I dedicated the second half of my internship to analyzing wastewater treatment facilities across California and their potential to adopt Combined Heat and Power (CHP) systems, focusing on the characteristics that make such an investment viable.

blocks.title: How Do Wastewater Treatment Plants Work?
blocks.body:
A wastewater treatment plant speeds up the natural processes through which water purifies itself. (EPA, 5) Wastewater moves through physical and biological treatment processes that remove debris, solids, organic matter, nutrients, pathogens, and other pollutants. A facility can be understood as having two connected pathways: a liquid treatment train that cleans the water and a solids treatment train that manages the sludge removed during treatment (Turn2engineering).
The liquid treatment process begins with primary treatment, which removes coarse solids from the wastewater. The wastewater then enters secondary treatment, where microorganisms break down much of the remaining organic matter. Secondary treatment can remove up to 90 percent of organic matter, with suspended growth processes such as activated sludge using oxygen-rich conditions to support microorganisms that consume organic material (EPA, 11). As these microorganisms grow, some are returned to the process while excess biomass is removed as waste activated sludge.

blocks.body: This sludge becomes the key connection between wastewater treatment and energy production. Primary treatment produces primary sludge, while biological treatment produces waste activated sludge containing water, organic material, microorganisms, and concentrated pollutants. After thickening removes some of the water, the sludge can undergo digestion to stabilize its organic solids (Turn2engineering). Anaerobic digestion can produce biogas, a methane-rich fuel that can be captured and used for energy generation. This creates the pathway from wastewater treatment to CHP: sludge → anaerobic digestion → biogas → electricity and useful heat (Turn2engineering).

blocks.title: How Do Combined Heat & Power Systems Work?
blocks.body: Combined heat and power (CHP) systems generate electricity and useful thermal energy from the same fuel source (Bhuva, 12). Instead of producing electricity and heat separately, CHP captures heat that would otherwise be lost during electricity generation, increasing overall efficiency and potentially lowering operating costs. CHP can also improve energy reliability and reduce emissions compared with separate electricity and heating systems (Bhuva, 14). At a wastewater treatment plant, the fuel can come directly from the treatment process.

Anaerobic digesters produce methane-rich biogas that can be used as CHP fuel, and more than 80 percent of WWTP CHP systems use biogas. The most common CHP technology at these facilities is the reciprocating engine, although microturbines, gas turbines, and fuel cells are also used (Bhuva, 16). In a typical reciprocating-engine or turbine CHP system, the fuel is combusted in a prime mover connected to an electrical generator. The generator produces electricity, while heat from the engine's exhaust and cooling system is recovered and used for the facility's thermal needs (Bhuva, 12). At WWTPs with anaerobic digesters, this allows the plant to use its own biogas to generate electricity and provide heat for operations such as digestion, while reducing dependence on outside energy sources. CHP can provide onsite power, reduce energy costs, and help WWTPs maintain operations during grid outages (Bhuva, 17). In this way, anaerobic digestion turns a wastewater treatment byproduct into an energy resource that can support both the plant's electricity and heat demands.

blocks.title: Wastewater Treatment Facilities Across  California
blocks.body:
To identify wastewater treatment plants across California and examine their connection to combined heat and power (CHP), I combined two geospatial datasets. The first was a California Wastewater Treatment Facility Dataset published through the CalOES GIS Data Manager, which provided point locations for facilities across the state. California Wastewater Treatment Facilities dataset The second was the U.S. Department of Energy's Onsite Energy Installation Database, which contains locations and information on onsite energy systems, including CHP facilities. 
Neither dataset was treated as a perfect inventory. The wastewater dataset included records labeled “Unknown,” facilities that appeared to have been retired, and other inconsistencies, while the CHP dataset did not always use the same facility names or classifications as the wastewater dataset. I therefore cleaned and standardized the records as much as possible before using them for the spatial analysis.

blocks.title: Case Study: East Bay Municipal Utility District Wastewater Treatment Plant

blocks.body: The East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) in Oakland, California, provides a good example of combined heat and power integration at a wastewater treatment plant. Serving approximately 650,000 customers and treating roughly 75 million gallons of wastewater per day, EBMUD began generating electricity from digester gas in 1985 and later expanded the system with a 4.6-MW gas turbine in 2011 (EBMUD, 1). The facility now produces an average of 6 MW of renewable electricity using methane-rich biogas generated during anaerobic digestion, making it the first wastewater treatment facility in North America to become a net energy producer and sell excess electricity back to the grid (EBMUD, 1). The CHP system achieves an overall efficiency of approximately 80%, saves an estimated $1.2 million annually in energy costs, and utilizes all recoverable waste heat for digester heating, demonstrating how wastewater treatment can be transformed from an energy-intensive process into an energy-generating resource (EBMUD, 1).

EBMUD also illustrates the technical process that makes CHP viable at wastewater treatment plants. Wastewater solids are stabilized in anaerobic digesters, where bacteria break down organic matter and produce digester gas composed of approximately 65% methane and 35% carbon dioxide (EMBUD, 2). After cleaning and conditioning, this biogas is used as fuel for turbines and engines that generate electricity, while the waste heat produced during generation is captured and returned to the digesters. To further increase biogas production, EBMUD accepts high-strength organic wastes such as fats, oils, and grease (FOG), which significantly enhance methane generation. As a result, the facility now generates between 110% and 140% of its own energy demand and can export surplus power to the grid (EMBUD, 2). This case demonstrates that CHP is most successful when a wastewater treatment plant has substantial anaerobic digestion capacity, reliable biogas production, and a consistent demand for both electricity and thermal energy.

blocks.title: Analysis
blocks.body:
While many factors impact whether a wastewater treatment plant is a viable candidate for a combined heat and power (CHP) upgrade, this analysis was intended as a preliminary screening exercise rather than a comprehensive assessment. The metric I focused on was whether the wastewater treatment plant has an anaerobic digester as without one, the system will not produce biogas to be used for fuel. Thus I searched for this information for each facility and documented the web source(s) used to support each data point. If a digester was identified, additional metrics such as digester gas production and  biogas flaring could be investigated in a more detailed analysis but that was beyond the scope of what I decided to do. 
Futhermore, I conducted a basic geospatial analysis to identify the Electric Load Serving Entity associated with each facility. I then cross-referenced the identified utility with the 2024 Utility Bundled Retail Sales dataset published by the U.S. Energy Information Administration to obtain the corresponding electricity rate. While this isn't a defensible use for actual regional electricity data, I wanted to leverage the geospatial platfrom to perform at least one points-in-polygon based analysis.

The results of this preliminary analysis revealed a striking truth: the majority of wastewater treatment plants within California aren't equipped with anaerobic digesters to make them eligable to even consider upgrading to a CHP system.
From the 254 facilities I identified as not having CHP, 54 of them indicated from web searches that they had anaerobic digesters. Another 195 facilities were too either too small to warrent that system, had other non-digestion solids management solutions, or didn't process solids on-site and so they sent it to bigger regional facilities that could process them. 5 of them were inconclusive. Futhermore, the results of the electrical rate geospatial analsyis is also in the data, however many facilites were situated in locations with overlapping electric service territories, so those remain inconclusive.

blocks.title: Financing a Combined Heat & Power Upgrades
blocks.body: While a viable plan for an actual upgrade is a multi-year process, here's some information on the process of paying for such an investment. Financing a CHP upgrade at a wastewater treatment plant can take several forms depending on the project's size, available capital, and ownership structure. CHP systems typically require an initial investment of approximately $700 to $3,000 per kW, but these costs can be recovered over time through energy savings (EPA, 1). Potential financing sources include local or state bonds, partnerships with utilities or third-party operators, and state or federal loans and grants. One particularly relevant option is the Clean Water State Revolving Fund (CWSRF), which provides low-interest financing for wastewater infrastructure and has been used specifically to fund CHP systems and upgrades to anaerobic digesters. CWSRF loans can have repayment periods of up to 30 years or the useful life of the project, while states can offer interest rates below market rates or other forms of financial assistance (EPA, 3). This makes CWSRF financing a potentially important mechanism for helping wastewater treatment plants overcome the upfront capital cost of CHP while using future energy savings to support the project's long-term economics.

blocks.title: Conclusion & Next Steps
blocks.body:
Overall, this analysis focused on identifying which wastewater treatment facilities in California may have the potential to upgrade to Combined Heat & Power (CHP). The initial dataset was developed by cross-referencing the U.S. Department of Energy’s Onsite Energy Installation Database with the CalOES GIS Data Manager to identify facilities that already have CHP systems and remove them from consideration. Web searches were then conducted for the remaining facilities to determine whether they have anaerobic digesters, a key feature for CHP because they can produce the biogas needed to generate energy. This screening found that roughly one-fifth of the facilities had evidence of an anaerobic digester. Starting with approximately 370 facilities and narrowing the list to roughly 50 of the most promising candidates through data screening and geospatial analysis provides a focused starting point for further investigation.
The next step would be to contact these approximately 50 facilities to verify the information collected and gather additional metrics needed to determine whether a CHP upgrade is technically and economically viable. These could include average daily flow, digester gas production, electricity rates, current biogas use or flaring, and other facility-specific operating data. More broadly, this analysis reinforced the importance of clean data, transparent sourcing, and verification. Public datasets provide a useful starting point for quickly screening a large number of facilities, but they should not be treated as a substitute for facility-level verification. The goal of this initial analysis was therefore not to determine exactly which facilities should receive CHP upgrades, but to efficiently narrow a large universe of facilities into a smaller group that can be investigated in greater depth.
